smt-2023-guts-01.title: Solve the absolute value inequality
smt-2023-guts-01.body:
$\widehat F-F=2C+30-\frac95C-32=\frac C5-2$. So $|\frac C5-2|\le5$ means $-5\le\frac C5-2\le5$, i.e. $-15\le C\le35$.

**Answer: $(-15,35)$**

smt-2023-guts-02.title: Bound and use last digits
smt-2023-guts-02.body:
The number has $20$ digits, far fewer than $23$, so $x<10$. It is odd, so $x$ is odd. The last digits of $1^{23},3^{23},5^{23},7^{23},9^{23}$ are $1,7,5,3,9$. The number ends in $3$, so $x=7$.

**Answer: 7**

smt-2023-guts-03.title: Classify by the ending
smt-2023-guts-03.body:
A valid sequence of length $n+1$ ends in $T$ (the first $n$ flips form any valid sequence: $S(n)$ ways), or in $TH$ ($S(n-1)$ ways), or in $THH$ ($S(n-2)$ ways). So $S(n+1)=S(n)+S(n-1)+S(n-2)$, giving $|a_0|+|a_1|+|a_2|=3$.

**Answer: 3**

smt-2023-guts-03.title: Subtract the bad extensions
smt-2023-guts-03.body:
Adding $T$ to any valid sequence stays valid; adding $H$ is invalid exactly when the sequence ends in $THH$, which happens $S(n-3)$ times. So $S(n+1)=2S(n)-S(n-3)$, with $\sum|a_n|=2+1=3$ as well.

**Answer: 3**

smt-2023-guts-04.title: Use the multiple-of-11 structure
smt-2023-guts-04.body:
For a three-digit multiple of $11$ we have $\overline{abc}=11n$ with $10\le n\le90$, and $11n=10n+n$. If there is no carry when adding $10n$ and $n$, then $b=a+c$ and the discriminant is $b^2-4ac=(a+c)^2-4ac=(a-c)^2\ge0$, so the roots are real. If a carry occurs, then $b=a+c-10$ (with the carry into the hundreds), so $b<a$ and $b<c$, and then $b^2<4ac$: no real roots.

So we count $n\in[10,90]$ whose digit sum is at most $9$ (no carry): for tens digit $t=1,\dots,8$ the units digit ranges over $0,\dots,9-t$, giving $9+8+\cdots+2=44$, plus $n=90$, total $45$.

**Answer: 45**

smt-2023-guts-05.title: Track the layers
smt-2023-guts-05.body:
$AB^2+BC^2=AC^2$, so $\angle B=90^\circ$ and $\angle C=60^\circ$. After the first fold, $A'$ lies on ray $BC$ beyond $C$ (since $BA'=\sqrt3>1$). The folded triangle $A'BD$ covers $\triangle BCD$ a second time, and sticks out as $\triangle A'CD$. Folding $\triangle A'CD$ over $CD$ lays it back over $\triangle BCD$, and the region where all three layers meet is a triangle $CDE$, a $30$-$60$-$90$ triangle with hypotenuse $CD$.

By the angle bisector theorem $CD=\frac{BC}{BC+BA}\cdot AC=\frac{2}{1+\sqrt3}$. Then $CE=CD\sin30^\circ=\frac1{1+\sqrt3}$ and $DE=CD\cos30^\circ=\frac{\sqrt3}{1+\sqrt3}$, so the area is $\frac12\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{(1+\sqrt3)^2}=\frac{\sqrt3}{2(4+2\sqrt3)}=\frac{2\sqrt3-3}{4}$.

**Answer: $\frac{2\sqrt3-3}4$**

smt-2023-guts-06.title: Sum of $i^3-i$
smt-2023-guts-06.body:
The sum is $\sum_{i=2}^{19}(i-1)i(i+1)=\sum_{i=1}^{19}(i^3-i)$ (the $i=1$ term is $0$). Using $\sum i^3=\left(\frac{n(n+1)}2\right)^2$ and $\sum i=\frac{n(n+1)}2$ with $n=19$: $190^2-190=190\cdot189=35910$.

**Answer: 35910**

smt-2023-guts-07.title: Count paths
smt-2023-guts-07.body:
Given that it reaches $(20,23)$, each of the $\binom{43}{20}$ lattice paths is equally likely. Those through $(20,20)$ number $\binom{40}{20}\cdot1$ (the last three steps are forced). The required probability is $1-\frac{\binom{40}{20}}{\binom{43}{20}}=1-\frac{23\cdot22\cdot21}{43\cdot42\cdot41}=1-\frac{253}{1763}=\frac{1510}{1763}$.

**Answer: $\frac{1510}{1763}$**

smt-2023-guts-09.title: Pythagorean theorem on centers
smt-2023-guts-09.body:
Put the base along the $x$-axis with the box from $x=0$ to $5$. The lower circles have centers $(1,1)$ and $(4,1)$; the upper circles have centers $(1,h)$ and $(4,h)$, where $h$ is the height at which they touch the sides. The middle circle has center $(\frac52,m)$ and is tangent to all four others.

Tangency to a lower circle: $\left(\frac32\right)^2+(m-1)^2=4$, so $m=1+\frac{\sqrt7}2$. Tangency to an upper circle: $\left(\frac32\right)^2+(h-m)^2=4$, so $h=m+\frac{\sqrt7}2=1+\sqrt7$.

**Answer: $1+\sqrt7$**

smt-2023-guts-10.title: Area equation and Simon's Favorite Factoring Trick
smt-2023-guts-10.body:
The areas give $3(2X)+4Y=3XY$, i.e. $3XY-6X-4Y=0$. Multiply by $3$ and factor: $(3X-4)(3Y-6)=24$.

We need $3X-4\equiv2\pmod3$ and $3Y-6\equiv0\pmod3$. Factor pairs of $24$ with first factor $\equiv2\pmod3$ and second a multiple of $3$ (positive $X$, $Y$): $(8,3)$ and $(2,12)$, giving $(X,Y)=(4,3)$ and $(2,6)$. (Negative factor pairs would give $X\le1$ with $3X-4<0$: $3X-4=-1$ gives $X=1$ and $3Y-6=-24$, $Y<0$, impossible.)

The sum of the possible $X$ is $4+2=6$.

**Answer: 6**

smt-2023-guts-11.title: Factor $(x-1)(y-1)$
smt-2023-guts-11.body:
Let the integer roots be $x,y$. Then $b=xy$ and $a=-(x+y)$, so $xy-(x+y)=1000$, i.e. $(x-1)(y-1)=1001=7\cdot11\cdot13$. Also $b=xy=1000+(x+y)$, so we minimize $x+y$.

If $x-1,y-1$ are positive the sum is at least about $2\sqrt{1001}$, giving $b>1000$; so take both negative: $x-1=-u$, $y-1=-v$ with $uv=1001$, and $x+y=2-(u+v)$, so $b=1002-(u+v)$ and we want $u+v$ as large as possible subject to $b>0$. $(u,v)=(1,1001)$ gives $b=0$ (not allowed). Next is $(7,143)$, giving $b=1002-150=852$ (check: $x=-6,y=-142$, $xy=852$, $-(x+y)=148=a$, $a+b=1000$).

**Answer: 852**

smt-2023-guts-12.title: The four numbers are consecutive
smt-2023-guts-12.body:
Two diagonal numbers differ by at most $4$ (via the triangle inequality along two sides). If they differed by $4$, the other two numbers would both have to lie between them at distance $2$ from each end, i.e. be equal: impossible. So all differences are at most $3$, and since the four numbers are distinct, they are four consecutive numbers $a,a+1,a+2,a+3$, with $a$ and $a+3$ diagonal.

Choose $a\in\{0,\dots,6\}$ ($7$ ways), the position of $a$ ($4$ ways) and of $a+1$ ($2$ ways); the rest is forced. Favorable: $7\cdot8$. Total ordered arrangements: $10\cdot9\cdot8\cdot7$. Probability $\frac{56}{5040}=\frac1{90}$.

**Answer: $\frac1{90}$**

smt-2023-guts-13.title: Coordinates
smt-2023-guts-13.body:
Put $A=(0,0)$, $B=(1,0)$, $C=\left(\frac12,\frac{\sqrt3}2\right)$. The second intersection $D$ of $\Omega_A$ and $\Omega_C$ is the reflection of $B$ over $AC$, namely $D=\left(-\frac12,\frac{\sqrt3}2\right)$; likewise $E$, the reflection of $A$ over $BC$, is $\left(\frac32,\frac{\sqrt3}2\right)$.

Then $\vec{BD}=\left(-\frac32,\frac{\sqrt3}2\right)$ has length $\sqrt3$, so $F=B+\frac{\vec{BD}}{\sqrt3}=\left(1-\frac{\sqrt3}2,\frac12\right)$, and similarly $G=\left(\frac{\sqrt3}2,\frac12\right)$. Lines $BD$ and $AE$ are medians-like lines through the centroid: $H=\left(\frac12,\frac{\sqrt3}6\right)$.

Line $CH$ is $x=\frac12$ and line $FG$ is $y=\frac12$, so $I=\left(\frac12,\frac12\right)$ and $IH=\frac12-\frac{\sqrt3}6=\frac{3-\sqrt3}6$.

**Answer: $\\frac{3-\\sqrt3}{6}$**

smt-2023-guts-14.title: Condition on positions
smt-2023-guts-14.body:
The second largest row maximum is $2023$ exactly when $2025$ and $2024$ are in the same row and $2023$ is in a different row.

Given the position of $2025$, the probability that $2024$ is in the same row is $\frac{44}{2024}$. Given that, the probability that $2023$ is in a different row is $\frac{2025-45}{2023}=\frac{1980}{2023}$.

The probability is $\frac{44\cdot1980}{2024\cdot2023}=\frac{990}{23\cdot7\cdot17^2}=\frac{990}{46529}$ in lowest terms ($2024=2^3\cdot11\cdot23$, $2023=7\cdot17^2$), so $p=990$.

**Answer: 990**

smt-2023-guts-15.title: Force the values one by one
smt-2023-guts-15.body:
Every $a$ divides $0$, so $f(a)\mid f(0)$ for all $a$; this forces $f(0)=0$. Since $1$ divides everything, $f(1)$ divides all $f(b)$, so $f(1)=1$. Next, $f(2)$ must divide $f(b)$ for $6$ values $b$ (namely $0,2,4,6,8,10$) and $f(3)$ for $4$ values ($0,3,6,9$); matching these counts forces $f(2)=2$, $f(3)=3$ and then $f(6)=6$.

$f(5)\mid f(10)$ leaves $(f(5),f(10))=(5,10)$ or $(4,8)$. The latter forces $f(4)=5$ and $f(8)=10$, contradicting $f(2)\mid f(4)$. So $f(5)=5$, $f(10)=10$, then $f(4)=4$, $f(8)=8$, $f(9)=9$. The only freedom is swapping the values of $7$ and $11$: $2$ functions. (A computer search confirms $2$.)

**Answer: 2**

smt-2023-guts-16.title: Factor $v$ and count preimages
smt-2023-guts-16.body:
$v(s)=s(s-1)(s+1)(s+4)(s+5)$, so Eric is stationary when $s(t)\in\{-5,-4,-1,0,1\}$.

$s(t)=t^3-3t^2$ increases up to a local maximum $s(0)=0$, decreases to a local minimum $s(2)=-4$, then increases. Counting distinct real solutions of $s(t)=c$: $c=-5$: $1$; $c=-4$: $2$ ($t=-1$ and $t=2$); $c=-1$: $3$; $c=0$: $2$ ($t=0,3$); $c=1$: $1$.

Total $1+2+3+2+1=9$.

**Answer: 9**

smt-2023-guts-17.title: Angle chase
smt-2023-guts-17.body:
Let $\beta=\angle ABC=45^\circ$, $\gamma=\angle ACB=60^\circ$. Both $N$ and $O_c$ lie on the perpendicular bisector of $AP$, which meets $AP$ at $M$.

Since $ABPH$ is cyclic, $\angle QHA=180^\circ-\angle AHP=\angle ABP=\beta$, and $\angle CAH=90^\circ-\gamma$. Hence $\angle CQP=\angle CAH+\angle QHA=90^\circ-\gamma+\beta$. As $N$ is the circumcenter of $AQP$, $\angle CQP=180^\circ-\angle AQP=\frac12\angle ANP=\angle MNP$.

Since $\angle AHB=180^\circ-\gamma$, the central angle is $\angle AO_cB=2\gamma$, so in the isosceles triangle $AO_cB$ $\angle O_cBA=90^\circ-\gamma$ and $\angle O_cBP=90^\circ-\gamma+\beta=\angle MNP$. Therefore $N,O_c,B,P$ are concyclic.

Since $O_cP=O_cB$, $\angle PO_cB=180^\circ-2\angle O_cBP=2(\gamma-\beta)$. Also $\angle APC=\gamma$ and $\angle NPA=90^\circ-\angle MNP=\gamma-\beta$, so $\angle NPC=2\gamma-\beta$, and in the cyclic quadrilateral $\angle NO_cB=2\gamma-\beta$. Hence $\angle NO_cP=\angle NO_cB-\angle PO_cB=\beta=45^\circ$. (A coordinate computation confirms $45^\circ$.)

**Answer: $45^\circ$**

smt-2023-guts-18.title: AM-GM with four terms
smt-2023-guts-18.body:
Write $3x+y=3x+\frac y3+\frac y3+\frac y3$. By AM-GM, $\frac{3x+\frac y3+\frac y3+\frac y3}{4}\ge\sqrt[4]{3x\cdot\frac{y^3}{27}}=\sqrt[4]{\frac{xy^3}{9}}=\sqrt[4]{\frac{16}{81}}=\frac23$. So $3x+y\ge\frac83$, with equality when $3x=\frac y3$, i.e. $y=9x$: $x=\frac29$, $y=2$.

**Answer: $\frac83$**

smt-2023-guts-19.title: Inclusion-exclusion
smt-2023-guts-19.body:
In circle $(A_1A_2O)$, $\angle A_1OA_2=30^\circ$ and $A_1A_2=1$, so the radius is $\frac{1}{2\sin30^\circ}=1$. Each circle passes through $O$ and has its center at distance $1$ from $O$; the six centers are $60^\circ$ apart, forming a regular hexagon around $O$.

Two circles with adjacent centers (distance $1$) overlap in a lens of area $\frac{2\pi}3-\frac{\sqrt3}2$. Circles with centers $120^\circ$ apart (distance $\sqrt3$) overlap in a lens of area $\frac\pi3-\frac{\sqrt3}2$, and this lens lies inside the circle between them, so it is also the triple intersection of three consecutive circles. Opposite circles only touch at $O$.

Inclusion-exclusion: the $120^\circ$ lenses are subtracted once as pairs and added back once as triples, so they cancel, leaving $6\pi-6\left(\frac{2\pi}3-\frac{\sqrt3}2\right)=2\pi+3\sqrt3$. (A numerical grid check of the union gives $11.479$, matching.)

**Answer: $2\\pi+3\\sqrt3$**

smt-2023-guts-20.title: Use $1000\equiv-1\pmod{13}$
smt-2023-guts-20.body:
Since $1001=7\cdot11\cdot13$, $1000\equiv-1\pmod{13}$. Write $N=2\cdot10^{2022}+x\cdot10^{22}+23$.

$10^{2022}=1000^{674}\equiv(-1)^{674}=1$, so $2\cdot10^{2022}\equiv2$. $10^{22}=10\cdot1000^7\equiv-10$, so $x\cdot10^{22}\equiv-10x$.

Thus $N\equiv2-10x+23=25-10x\pmod{13}$. We need $10x\equiv25\equiv12\pmod{13}$; since $10\cdot4=40\equiv1$, $x\equiv12\cdot4=48\equiv9$. So $x=9$.

**Answer: 9**

smt-2023-guts-21.title: Only the first arrival's waiting time matters
smt-2023-guts-21.body:
Suppose they arrive $x$ minutes apart. They meet iff the earlier arrival waits at least $x$ minutes, which has probability $\max\left(0,\frac{30-x}{30}\right)$. The gap $x=|a-b|$ of two uniform arrival times on $[0,60]$ has density $\frac{2(60-x)}{60^2}$.

$P=\int_0^{30}\frac{30-x}{30}\cdot\frac{2(60-x)}{3600}\,dx=\frac1{30}\int_0^{30}\left(1-\frac x{30}\right)\left(1-\frac x{60}\right)dx=\frac1{30}\left[30-\frac{900}{40}+\frac{27000}{5400}\right]=\frac{12.5}{30}=\frac5{12}$.

**Answer: $\frac5{12}$**

smt-2023-guts-22.title: Constant on blocks
smt-2023-guts-22.body:
Let $S_k=\{2023^k,\dots,2023^{k+1}-1\}$. For $n\in S_k$, the three indices lie in $S_{k-1},S_{k-2},S_{k-3}$ (or are $0$), so $A_n$ is constant on each $S_k$; call the value $B_k$. For $1\le n<2023$ all three terms are $A_0=1$, so $B_0=3$. Then $B_k=B_{k-1}+B_{k-2}+B_{k-3}$, with the missing terms equal to $A_0=1$.

$B_0=3$, $B_1=3+1+1=5$, $B_2=5+3+1=9$, $B_3=17$, $B_4=31$, $B_5=57$, $B_6=105$, $B_7=193$, $B_8=355$, $B_9=653$.

The index $2023^9+20$ lies in $S_9$, so the answer is $653$.

**Answer: 653**

smt-2023-guts-23.title: Napoleon's triangle
smt-2023-guts-23.body:
$\triangle A_2B_2C_2$ is equilateral (Napoleon's theorem: $\triangle AB_2C_2\sim\triangle AB_1B$ with ratio $1:\sqrt3$, and similarly for the others). Since $5^2+8^2-5\cdot8=49=7^2$, the angle between the sides of length $5$ and $8$ is $60^\circ$; let it be at $A$, with $AC=5$ and $AB=8$. Then $AB_2=\frac{5}{\sqrt3}$, $AC_2=\frac8{\sqrt3}$ (circumradii of the equilateral triangles on $AC$ and $AB$) and $\angle B_2AC_2=60^\circ+30^\circ+30^\circ=120^\circ$.

Law of Cosines: $B_2C_2^2=\frac{25}3+\frac{64}3+\frac{40}3=43$. The area is $\frac{\sqrt3}{4}\cdot43=\frac{43\sqrt3}4$.

**Answer: $\frac{43\sqrt3}{4}$**

smt-2023-guts-24.title: Linearity of expectation
smt-2023-guts-24.body:
An untagged person stays untagged iff none of the $10$ taggers lands on their vertex, which has probability $\left(\frac{19}{20}\right)^{10}$. So $E=10\left(\frac{19}{20}\right)^{10}=\frac{19^{10}}{2\cdot20^9}=\frac{19^{10}}{2^{19}\cdot5^9}$, already in lowest terms.

Thus $a+b=19^{10}+2\cdot20^9=6131066257801+1024000000000=7155066257801$.

**Answer: $19^{10}+2\cdot20^9=7155066257801$**

smt-2023-guts-25.title: Zigzag numbers
smt-2023-guts-25.body:
The conditions say $\pi(1)<\pi(2)>\pi(3)<\pi(4)>\cdots$, so $N$ is the Euler zigzag number $E_{1000}$ (up-down permutations of length $1000$). Classically $E_n\sim2\left(\frac2\pi\right)^{n+1}n!$.

Taking $\log_{10}$: $\log_{10}1000!\approx2567.60$ (consistent with the given $2568$ digits), $\log_{10}2\approx0.301$, and $1001\log_{10}\frac2\pi\approx-196.31$. So $\log_{10}N\approx2371.59$ and $N$ has $2372$ digits.

A cruder estimate: $N$ lies between $\frac{1000!}{2^{999}}$ and $\frac{1000!}{2^{500}}$, and guessing $\frac{1000!}{2^{750}}$ gives $2568-225=2343$, which would earn $19$ points. An exact dynamic program over the relative rank of the last element also gives $2372$.

**Official answer: $2372$**

smt-2023-guts-26.title: Estimate, then count exactly
smt-2023-guts-26.body:
The $n$-th product of three primes is about $\frac{2n\ln n}{(\ln\ln n)^2}$ (asymptotically), so numbers up to $10000$ number about $2704$ and up to $5000$ about $1353$: an estimate of $\approx1351$ (worth $16$ points).

An exact count enumerates triples of primes $p\le q\le r$ with $5000\le pqr\le10000$ (primes up to $2500$) and gives $1296$.

**Official answer: $1296$**

smt-2023-guts-27.title: Simulation
smt-2023-guts-27.body:
A direct simulation (choose $1000$ random distinct lattice points, find the largest set on one line, average over many trials) gives $N\approx6.02$, i.e. $\lfloor100N\rfloor=602$ (the official solution averaged $10^4$ trials; an independent run of $600$ trials gave a mean of $6.03$). A heuristic: lines with many lattice points are few, and the maximum collinear subset is usually $5$, $6$ or $7$ points.

**Official answer: $602$**
